comments.text:
Created attachment 3592
Unify messages in R-base.pot

I am experimenting a bit with using LLMs to identify messages in .pot files which should be unified. I think they are pretty well-suited to the task.

The attached patch has a first pass (low-hanging fruit) at R-base.pot (i.e., the messages generated from R in {bases}). Gemini identified the similar messages, and I edited the files.

Removing highly-correlated messages like this eases the burden on translation teams, who can avoid the tedium of translating ~the same message over and over. It also improves the end user experience by minimizing the opportunity for the same message to be translated slightly differently. The tradeoff is on the developers who have to keep this goal in mind when crafting messages. We might avoid this by adding a step to the translation release process that scans the sources for similar messages before any new extraction to .pot, so that only the translations maintainer needs to think too carefully about this.

Some further notes about the actual changes:

 - We have `invalid '%s'` and `invalid %s` separately, we might consider putting the `'` into the templated part to have only `invalid %s`. OTOH, `'` could be a useful signal to the translator, so I left it as is for now.
 - I landed on `'%s' is not` (i.e., wrapping with `'` and using "is") for consistency across the Date/POSIXt/difftime method messages like `'%s' is not defined for "%s" objects`
 - We have both `bad '%s' argument` and `invalid '%s' argument`, they could probably be unified to `invalid '%s' argument`.

Lastly, this exercise can easily be repeated:

 1. For all the individual .pot files in the R sources
 2. For identifying opportunities to re-use messages across the different domains (e.g. using `gettext("Invalid 'file' argument", domain="R-base")` in utils/R/* to avoid generating `Invalid 'file' argument` for independent translation in utils/po/R-utils.pot). This has a lot of opportunity to reduce duplicate translations of identical strings, but also has a lot of developer overhead.

---

SVN mirror CI run: https://github.com/r-devel/r-svn/pull/224
comments.creator: michaelchirico4

comments.text:
Thank you, Michael, for addressing this message translation issue more systematically.
I had myself done such unifications on a small scale basis, almost always when some part of the *code* was changed additionally.

However, I think you (as native English speaker, even though almost surely of Italian descent from your last name) are overlooking something (s.below);
in addition to that, I guess many (me included) would prefer being less "thorough" and favor simple source code, more.

Notably, this change, replacing
```
 stop("invalid 'dims'")
```
by
```
 stop(gettextf("invalid '%s'", "dims"), domain=NA)
```
seems to be too much "code bloat".  Translators really can globally replace
"invalid" by the correct word in their language, very quickly.

But I think there is one crucial oversight here: probably in quite a few languages (notably western European ones I "kind of" know), the translators additionally must adapt the adjective to the correct gender and plural/singular form, hence the ending (in the above cases) needs to be adapted in any case by the translator.
Even in the above example (where 'dims' is an argument name), one could argue that the adjective should reflect the plural, and indeed, e.g., currently, 
`src/library/base/po/R-es.po` has
```
msgid "invalid 'dims'"
msgstr "'dims' no válidas"
```
(the (LaTeX) v\'alidas  with 1 unicode character is not properly rendered in our bugzilla..)
using female plural "as" (matching Spanish "dimensi'ones" f, pl 
  [ 'o : our bugzilla doesn't render unicode accented characters correctly..])
Similarly for (almost?) all the half dozen languages I know well enough to know they use such endings.

Even though I'm grateful for your proposal, according to the above, I think your patch would need to become considerably smaller, before we'dconsider applying it.
comments.creator: maechler

comments.text:
(In reply to Martin Maechler from comment #1)
> But I think there is one crucial oversight here: probably in quite a few
> languages (notably western European ones I "kind of" know), the translators
> additionally must adapt the adjective to the correct gender and
> plural/singular form, hence the ending (in the above cases) needs to be
> adapted in any case by the translator.

When dealing with symbols, like `dims` in `gettext("invalid 'dims'")` or `gettextf("invalid '%s'", "dims")`, I think that code authors could simplify the work of translators by writing, e.g., `gettextf("invalid argument '%s'", "dims")`, leading unambiguously to a singular declension of the adjective "invalid".  That seems appropriate, too, because if `typeof(dims)` is invalid, then it is really the singular object-as-a-whole that is invalid, rather than some set of component "dimensions".  The plural declension seems misleading in this case.

When dealing with calls, like `nrow(x)` in `gettext("invalid nrow(x)")` or `gettextf("invalid %s", "nrow(x)")`, I would agree that the former is often better for translation, because the noun being modified by "invalid" is implied by the function name ("number" in "number of rows").  I guess that code authors can avoid some repetition with `gettextf("invalid nrow(%s)", "x")`, since it is sufficient that translators have the name of the outermost function, but then I am sympathetic to Martin's comment about thoroughness at the cost of compactness.
comments.creator: jaganmn2

comments.text:
> Translators really can globally replace "invalid" by the correct word in their language, very quickly.

I get your point, and am a bit allergic to all the cruft around the updated code as well, but here are some other considerations:

 - Increasingly, translation is done by teams -- global find-and-replace requires the same translator does all of the similar strings, which may be hard to enforce.
 - It's also harder to enforce the same translation _across_ domains (like 'R-utils' or 'grDevices', ...). The patch here doesn't address that directly, but the proposed process gets us closer to enabling that
 - Bug #18280 would reduce the boilerplate overhead a bit by pushing the `gettextf()` part "under the hood"

> the translators additionally must adapt the adjective to the correct gender and plural/singular form, hence the ending (in the above cases) needs to be adapted in any case by the translator.

This is definitely a blind spot for me as an English native -- Ivan Krylov has definitely improved my instincts here a bit, but I still have a ways to go. As Mikael pointed out, `'dims'` in particular is tricky -- it's a code argument, does it automatically get the same handling as the plain English word? It might be a matter of taste.

Anyway, it does lend itself to an extension of the initial prompt -- something that we could build on iteratively.

Current prompt:

```
You are an expert Localization Engineer and Linguist. Your goal is to optimize the translation template file @R-base.pot by identifying
  strings that can be unified into templates.

  Please follow these steps:

  1.  **Extraction & Analysis:**
      * Analyze the content of @R-base.pot.
      * Focus on `msgid` entries, ignoring headers and metadata.
      * Identify pairs or groups of strings that are semantically identical except for specific variables (punctuation, variable nouns,
  numbers).
      * Propose a unified template string (e.g., unify "Hello 'World'" and "Hello 'User'" into "Hello '%s'").

  2.  **Multilingual Viability Check (Simulation):**
      * For each proposed unification, perform a linguistic structural check.
      * **Context:** You do not need to provide professional translations. You are simulating the logic of grammar to see if the template
  breaks.
      * Simulate how the unified string would behave in German, Spanish, Russian, Japanese, and Arabic.
      * **Criteria:** Check for issues with word order, gender agreement, and declension/pluralization that would make the template impossible
  to use in those languages.
      * *Example of failure:* If a noun is hardcoded in English but affects the adjective's ending in Russian, the template is invalid.
      * Discard any proposals that fail this check.

  3.  **Output:**
      * List the surviving candidates. Show the original strings and the proposed unified template.
```

And indeed, it winds up excluding many of the original changes, such as the 'invalid %s' originally proposed:

```
Based on the analysis of the R-base.pot file, here are the recommended unification candidates that have passed a multilingual viability
  check.

  1. Mutually Exclusive Options

  Analysis:
  The file contains multiple strings indicating that two options are mutually exclusive. These strings are identical in structure, only
  differing in the names of the options.

   * Original Strings:

   1     msgid "\"all\" and \"exact\" are mutually exclusive"
   2     msgid "\"hexNumeric\" and \"digits17\" are mutually exclusive"

   * Proposed Unified Template:
   1     "\"%s\" and \"%s\" are mutually exclusive"

  Multilingual Viability Check:
  This template is structurally sound across multiple languages. The placeholder substitutions do not interfere with grammar, word order, or
  agreement.

   * German: "%s" und "%s" schließen sich gegenseitig aus.
   * Spanish: "%s" y "%s" son mutuamente excluyentes.
   * Russian: "%s" и "%s" являются взаимоисключающими.
   * Japanese: 「%s」と「%s」は互いに排他的です。
   * Arabic: "%s" و "%s" حصريان بشكل متبادل.

  Conclusion: This unification is viable and recommended.

  2. Operations Not Defined for Object Types

  Analysis:
  There are many strings stating that a certain operation is not defined for a specific object type (e.g., "Date", "POSIXt", "difftime"). These
  can be consolidated into a single template. A minor normalization of the source strings (e.g., ensuring "is not defined" is used
  consistently) might be needed.

   * Original Strings (selection):

   1     msgid "binary + is not defined for \"Date\" objects"
   2     msgid "unary - is not defined for \"Date\" objects"
   3     msgid "%s not defined for \"Date\" objects"
   4     msgid "binary '+' is not defined for \"POSIXt\" objects"
   5     msgid "'%s' not defined for \"difftime\" objects"

   * Proposed Unified Template:
   1     "%s is not defined for \"%s\" objects"
      (This assumes source strings are normalized to include "is" for consistency.)

  Multilingual Viability Check:
  The structure holds across languages. The first placeholder (the operation) and the second placeholder (the object type) do not create
  grammatical conflicts in this sentence structure.

   * German: "%s ist nicht für \"%s\"-Objekte definiert."
   * Spanish: "%s no está definido para objetos de tipo \"%s\"."
   * Russian: "%s не определен для объектов типа \"%s\"."
   * Japanese: 「%s」は「%s」オブジェクトに対して定義されていません。
   * Arabic: "%s" غير معرّف لكائنات "%s".

  Conclusion: This unification is viable and recommended.

  3. Unification of Singular/Plural Messages

  Analysis:
  The file contains separate strings for singular and plural forms of the same message, which should be handled by the localization framework's
  pluralization support (e.g., ngettext).

   * Original Strings:

   1     msgid "'by' must match number of columns"
   2     msgid "'by' must match numbers of columns"

   * Proposed Unified Template (using `msgid_plural`):
      These should be merged into a single entry with plural forms.

   1     msgid "'by' must match %d column"
   2     msgid_plural "'by' must match %d columns"
      (Note: The original strings lack a number placeholder, which would need to be added in the source code to enable plural handling.)

  Multilingual Viability Check:
  All target languages (and modern localization frameworks) have robust support for pluralization rules. This is a standard localization
  practice that is universally viable.

  Conclusion: This is a highly recommended best-practice change. It correctly handles grammar and reduces string count.
```

Happy to update the patch if this makes more sense, as well as to try applying this to more .pot files if we're getting more comfortable with the true positive rate.
